title: Second-order cone lift dimension of semialgebraic convex hulls
formal: Determine the function \(a(S)\) giving the minimum number of auxiliary real scalar variables in an exact second-order cone representation of \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\), for every semialgebraic set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and every integer \(n\geq1\). Set \(a(S)=\infty\) when no finite such representation exists. For finite values, the benchmark accepts a real approximation within absolute error \(1/100\); infinite values require proof of nonrepresentability.
why: Second-order cone lifts expose nonlinear convex structure through a class of conic constraints with effective optimization methods. Understanding both representability and the minimum added dimension would distinguish intrinsic geometric obstacles from the overhead of particular reformulations, while keeping those questions separate from numerical relaxation quality.
status_note: The general characterization and auxiliary-dimension questions are open directions in the 2018 source. The individual review on 13 September 2026 checked major obstruction and positive-family results through 2025 but found no complete determination of the selected function. No exhaustive present-day openness certification is claimed.

importance.reason: A broad structural question about exact conic formulations, connecting real algebraic geometry with the extra dimension needed to represent convex optimization models.

sentences: A semialgebraic set is described by polynomial equalities and inequalities, while its convex hull collects all convex combinations of its points.
The source asks when that convex hull can be represented using second-order cone constraints and auxiliary variables.
It also asks how many additional variables such a representation requires.
Representability is stronger than having a useful numerical relaxation, because the projected feasible region must agree exactly with the desired hull.
A structural answer would identify nonlinear models that can be converted into a tractable conic formulation and quantify the cost of that conversion.

definitions: A semialgebraic set is one defined by a finite Boolean combination of polynomial equalities and strict or non-strict polynomial inequalities with real coefficients. Its convex hull is the set of all finite convex combinations of its points: \(\sum_{i=1}^t\lambda_i s_i\), where \(t\geq1\), \(s_i\in S\), \(\lambda_i\geq0\) and \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\). The convex hull of the empty set is empty. No closure is taken, and neither compactness nor closedness is assumed. For \(d\geq2\), the Lorentz cone is \(\mathcal L_d=\{(t,z)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{d-1}:t\geq\|z\|_2\}\); also let \(\mathcal L_1=\mathbb R_{\geq0}\). An admissible representation with \(r\in\mathbb N_0\) auxiliary variables has the form \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^r,\ E(x,y)=e,\ F_j(x,y)\in\mathcal L_{d_j}\ (1\leq j\leq N)\},\] where \(N\geq0\), all cone dimensions \(d_j\geq1\) are finite, \(E\) is a real linear map with finitely many rows, \(e\) is a real vector, and each \(F_j\) is a real affine map into \(\mathbb R^{d_j}\). There is no bound on the number or dimensions of the cones, the number of affine equations or coefficient sizes. The number \(r\) counts only the scalar coordinates of \(y\), not the original coordinates of \(x\), the number of constraints or their output dimensions. Let \(a(S)\) be the least such \(r\), or infinity if the set of admissible integers is empty. In particular, zero auxiliary variables are allowed. The domain consists of mathematical sets with their ambient dimension, not particular defining formulas; equivalent descriptions of the same set must give the same answer. Coefficients of both the input descriptions and the lifts may be arbitrary real numbers. This is a characterization problem, not a claim that arbitrary real coefficients have finite machine encodings.
answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular mathematical description or certified rule for \(a\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof identifying its infinite-value domain and giving a real-valued function \(g\) with \(|g(S)-a(S)|\leq1/100\) whenever \(a(S)<\infty\). A proved interval of width at most \(1/50\) may specify a finite answer through its midpoint. The approximation need not be integer-valued. Upper-bound constructions without matching minimality information, isolated representable families, or merely repeating the defining optimization over lifts are insufficient.

context_blocks.text: Section 5.1 of the 2018 Dagstuhl report asks both when a semialgebraic convex hull has a second-order cone representation and how many extra variables are necessary. The minimum-auxiliary-dimension function combines these into one target. The displayed model is an explicit editorial convention for “extra variables”; it permits all finite Lorentz-cone dimensions and real affine coefficients.

Allowing auxiliary variables can express convex sets that are not intersections of second-order cone constraints in their original coordinates. The number of auxiliary variables differs from conic extension complexity measured by the number of cones, their total dimension, or a semidefinite matrix block size. Those measures cannot silently replace a(S).

Fawzi proves that the cone of positive semidefinite real symmetric three-by-three matrices has no second-order cone representation. Thus even a semialgebraic convex set with a direct semidefinite description can have an infinite value here.

Scheiderer proves that every closed convex semialgebraic subset of the plane is second-order cone representable. This establishes finiteness for that class, but does not on its own give the minimum number of auxiliary variables for each member.

Scheiderer’s 2025 preprint proves representability for compact convex semialgebraic sets with Nash-smooth boundary of strictly positive curvature and for Nash-smooth hyperbolicity cones. These are substantial additional sufficient conditions, not a characterization of every set or its minimum auxiliary dimension.

Exact equality matters even for nonclosed hulls: linear projections of closed conic feasible sets need not be closed. Replacing a convex hull by its closure can therefore change the problem. Since this target leaves constraint counts unrestricted, a small auxiliary dimension alone is not a polynomial runtime guarantee.
